headline: From Prison Cell to Machine Shop: Ex-Cons Learn Trades, Transform Lives
meta_description: Rise Up Industries in San Diego gives formerly incarcerated men paid apprenticeships in CNC machining, with only 3% reoffending versus a national rate of 66%.
summary_short: A San Diego nonprofit is transforming lives by teaching formerly incarcerated men machinist skills through paid apprenticeships combined with therapy and mentorship.
body:
In a converted machine shop in southeastern San Diego, Rise Up Industries has spent over a decade turning felony records into machinist certifications. The program combines paid apprenticeships in CNC machining with therapy, tutoring, and case management—addressing what Executive Director Jonathan Yackley calls the reality that "technical training alone is not enough." Men who spent decades in prison now fill manufacturing contracts for aerospace, medical devices, and automotive parts, while supporting one another through the transition to life beyond bars. The impact is measurable: only 3% of program graduates re-offend compared to a national recidivism rate of roughly 66% over three years, according to the Bureau of Justice Statistics.

Komisi Savaiinaea, who served more than two decades in prison, exemplifies this transformation. Initially skeptical about learning machining with no prior experience, he found confidence by watching fellow participants succeed. He has since become a supervisor, now welcoming new apprentices with the credibility that only someone who has walked that same path can offer. Anthony Walkens, who completed 47 years of a 55-years-to-life sentence for gang-related homicide, describes arriving at Rise Up Industries as overwhelming—until Komisi and others reassured him he could succeed. "It's really a beautiful place," Walkens says, "kind of like a family setting."

What distinguishes Rise Up is its recognition that formerly incarcerated people face isolation, trauma, and instability alongside lack of opportunity. By pairing demanding career training with behavioral health support and a genuine community where participants know they belong, the program creates what Yackley calls "sustainable change." Komisi's own journey—supporting his wife through his own recovery while now supervising manufacturing teams—reveals how leadership skills forged in difficult circumstances can be redirected toward building something meaningful.
